idiom_name: Razor presentational component ([Parameter] in, EventCallback out) plus a container component that injects the data service
implementation_notes: In Blazor a component is an ordinary C# class, so the split is expressed in parameters: the presentational component declares [Parameter] properties for the values it renders and an EventCallback for each event it raises, and can be rendered from literal parameters in a test or a design-time harness, while the container component injects the data service, owns loading and error state and passes the result down. What replaces the classic container plumbing is the framework's own parameter and event-callback contract, with @bind for two-way UI state. Keep the container form where the component is the place that chooses the data source (a route or screen component), and prefer the MVVM variant in XAML stacks, where bindings already carry the values.
pitfalls: Copying a parameter into a field freezes the child on its first value; parameters arrive through the parameter-set lifecycle, so derive from them instead of caching them.
Loading or computing inside the render path repeats the work on every re-render; the supply half should load once and hand an immutable result down.
A child that mutates a collection it received as a parameter destroys the one-way flow the split depends on.

variants.name: MVVM: viewmodel as supply half, XAML view as binding document
variants.idiom_name: INotifyPropertyChanged viewmodel plus a XAML view that only binds
variants.implementation_notes: In WPF, WinUI and .NET MAUI the supply half is a viewmodel: it holds the data, exposes properties that raise PropertyChanged (and observable collections) and offers commands, while the view is a declarative binding document with no logic of its own - the binding engine is what passes values down and events up, so no wrapper component is needed. Keep framework-aware work (dispatcher, dialogs, navigation) out of the viewmodel so it stays unit-testable, and keep the view renderable from design-time data so it can be laid out without the application running.
pitfalls: Binding to a field, or to a property that never raises PropertyChanged, produces a view that does not update.
Viewmodels that hold dispatcher, control or context references leak UI concerns into the supply half and stop being headlessly testable.
Two-way bindings can quietly become a second source of truth when the view writes state the supply half never learns about.
